name: Hmwaveke
confidence_why: Known only second-hand, as quoted in another work.

catalog_locator: Rohleder 2024, sec. 5.6 Stress, p. 82; supporting passage sec. 5.3.1 Quantity, pp. 74-75. Campbell 1987 (the primary description Rohleder reports), sec. 5.2 Stress and length, pp. 56-59, held and quoted in this record.
catalog_quote: For Hmwaveke, stress is described as being fundamentally penultimate (Campbell 1987: 59), and forms which deviate from this, with few exceptions, are analyzed by Campbell as several phonological words. Campbell analyzes long syllables in plurisyllabic words as resulting from stress (suggesting that, fundamentally, length is a feature of all stressed syllables). For Vamale, though long syllables are stressed, I argue that the relation is reversedː length attracts stress. ... [pp. 74-75] This analysis is contested for Voh-Koné languages: Campbell analyzes long vowels in Hmwaveke polysyllabic words as a feature of the stressed syllable (Campbell 1987: 56). In cases where a fortis-onset syllable takes the stress despite other factors, like the presence of a long syllable (e.g. [ˈtʰa.keː.ke] ‘stretch out’), or a penultimate syllable (e.g. [’xaⁿ.ɟa.ke] ‘eat starchy food’), this is argued to be due to extra articulatory energy, but not phonologically stress (Campbell 1987: 59).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word; apparent departures are analysed as sequences of separate phonological words, and vowel/syllable length in polysyllables is treated as a consequence of stress rather than a trigger of it.
new_statements.exceptions: Forms deviating from penultimate stress are, 'with few exceptions', analysed as several phonological words; fortis-onset syllables that appear to take stress despite a long or penultimate syllable (e.g. [ˈtʰa.keː.ke] 'stretch out', ['xaⁿ.ɟa.ke] 'eat starchy food') are attributed to 'extra articulatory energy, but not phonologically stress' (Campbell 1987: 59, as reported on Rohleder p. 75).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: Campbell (per Rohleder) treats deviant forms as sequences of several phonological words, so the penultimate rule is stated over the phonological word; Rohleder adds that Campbell derives syllable length in polysyllables from stress. Second-hand: Rohleder's own sec. 5.6 describes Vamale (penultimate, weight-sensitive), and only this sentence reports Hmwaveke.
new_statements.identity_note: Campbell 1987 describes 'Fa Tieta' (fa tieta = 'language of Tiéta'), which Rivierre & Ehrhart 2006 (intro, via archive.org highlights) characterise as the idiom of Tiéta where Hmwaeke speakers have merged with the Hmwaveke; Glottolog files the thesis under Hmwaveke [hmwa1243, mrk], while Rohleder 2024 (p. 46) also calls Fa Tieta 'Hmwaeke' (Hmwaeke proper is otherwise the Vamale dialect, vama1243). Leenhardt 1946 ch. 28 ''Moavekè' (Voh, Tiéta) is the same variety. The scan's named source 'Haudricourt & Ozanne-Rivierre 1982 Dictionnaire thématique.. Voh-Koné' does not exist under that title (the 1982 dictionary is for the Hienghène region); the Voh-Koné/Tiéta dictionary is Rivierre's unpublished ms.

new_statements.quote: p. 56: "As mentioned in the preceding section, the nucleus of the phonological word is the stressed syllable. In Fa Tieta stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. This hypothesis may be adduced from the following examples: /'tana/ 'red' /'udu/ 'to drink' /we'dyati/ 'ocean' /ya'vato/ 'to ignite' /pu'theke/ 'to push'. Additional evidence confirming this hypothesis is furnished by the suffixation of the possessive pronouns to nouns: a stress shift is observable so that stress occurs on the penultimate syllable. For example: /'fwadi/ 'nose' ... /fwa'didye/ 'their noses' ... /'fedat/ 'blood' /fe'dalan/ 'his blood' /feda'ladye/ 'their blood'" -- p. 57: "In words of more than three syllables, secondary stress will occur two syllables before the primary stress." -- p. 59: "There is no stress shift, as primary stress remains on the penultimate syllable."

new_statements.relation_note: This is the primary source behind the catalog's penultimate record (which rests on Rohleder 2024 sec. 5.6 reporting Campbell 1987: 59). Read directly, it confirms fixed penultimate primary stress and adds detail the catalog lacks: secondary stress two syllables before the primary, allophonic lengthening of the stressed vowel, the three-syllable maximum for a simple phonological word, loanword re-stressing, and the compound / -aman exceptions. Note Rohleder's page '59' points at the 'no stress shift, primary stress remains on the penultimate' sentence; the main rule statement is on p. 56.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word; it is predictable (p. 62-63: 'it need not be marked phonemically as it is predictable') and demarcative, so a simple phonological word has at most three syllables (optional pre-nuclear syllable + stressed penult + one post-nuclear syllable, p. 55). Stress shifts rightward under possessive suffixation to stay penultimate ('fwadi > fwa'didye), and French loans are re-stressed to the penult ([le'di] > ['le:di] 'Monday'). The stressed vowel of a polysyllable is allophonically lengthened (p. 59). Monosyllables bear stress; affixed pronouns never carry word stress (p. 54).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 57: in words of more than three syllables secondary stress falls two syllables before the primary stress (["thamo'sian] 'young sister', ["sale'kade] 'whose', ["hale'lewa] 'cicada'); Campbell flags that these may in fact be two phonological words. pp. 58-59: an apparent initial secondary stress in trisyllables with a fortis initial consonant (["xa'hmaen] 'tomorrow') is attributed to fortis articulatory effort, not a stress shift.
new_statements.exceptions: sec. 5.3.2 pp. 63-64: compound words keep the stress of each component even when it is no longer penultimate (/ve'sili'ye/ 'drill', /ve'siti'sep/ 'coconut grater'), so they are analysed as more than one phonological word; a set of words in the suffix -aman (/vehwa'liaman/ 'fork') 'seems to have a stress pattern which does not conform to the penultimate stress rule, for reasons which have not been discovered yet'; in possessive derivations of such nouns stress does not shift.
new_statements.identity_note: Campbell describes 'Fa Tieta' ('language of Tieta'), the name chosen by the Tieta orthography committee for the speech of Tieta village (Voh-Kone area, west coast of northern New Caledonia). She states (pp. 1-2) that the founding clan's language is Hmwaveke, now 'being assimilated with Hmwaeke' so that speakers under 50-55 no longer distinguish the two, and that the community regards what it speaks as a hybrid; the thesis nonetheless opens 'The Hmwaveke language is spoken in the north region of the island of New Caledonia' and Glottolog/the catalog file it under Hmwaveke (hmwa1243). Data from six months' fieldwork in 1986 with Fa Tieta speakers in Tieta and Noumea.
